text:
At the gallop of four horses, she had been borne away for eight days toward a new country, from which they would never return. On they went, on they went, their arms entwined, without speaking. Often, from the top of a mountain, they would suddenly glimpse some splendid city with domes, bridges, ships, forests of lemon trees, and cathedrals of white marble, whose pointed steeples bore storks’ nests. They would proceed at a walk because of the great paving stones, and on the ground there were bouquets of flowers that women dressed in red bodices offered you. Bells could be heard ringing, mules neighing, along with the murmur of guitars and the sound of fountains, whose drifting spray cooled heaps of fruit arranged in pyramids at the feet of pale statues that smiled beneath the jets of water. And then, one evening, they would arrive at a fishing village, where brown nets dried in the wind along the cliff and the huts. It was there that they would stop to live; they would inhabit a low house with a flat roof, shaded by a palm tree, at the head of a gulf, on the seashore. They would go out in a gondola, they would sway in a hammock; and their existence would be easy and ample like their silk garments, all warm and starry like the mild nights they would contemplate. Yet, across the immensity of this future that she conjured up before herself, nothing particular arose; the days, all magnificent, resembled one another like waves; and it swayed on the horizon, infinite, harmonious, bluish, and bathed in sunlight.
But the child would begin coughing in her cradle, or Bovary would snore more loudly, and Emma would not fall asleep until morning, when dawn whitened the windowpanes and little Justin was already opening the shutters of the pharmacy on the square.

She had sent for Monsieur Lheureux and had said to him:

“I need a cloak, a large cloak, with a long collar, lined.”

“Are you going on a journey?” he asked.

“No! But... no matter, I am counting on you, am I not? And quickly!”

He bowed.

“I shall also need,” she resumed, “a trunk... not too heavy... convenient.”

“Yes, yes, I understand, about ninety-two centimeters by fifty, as they make them nowadays.”

“With an overnight bag.”

“There is definitely some trouble behind all this,” Lheureux thought.

“And here,” Madame Bovary said, drawing her watch from her belt, “take this; you can pay yourself out of it.”

But the merchant exclaimed that she was wrong; they knew each other; did he doubt her? What childishness! She nevertheless insisted that he take at least the chain, and Lheureux had already put it in his pocket and was leaving when she called him back.

“You will leave everything at your house. As for the cloak”—she appeared to reflect—“do not bring that either; just give me the workman’s address and tell him to keep it at my disposal.”

It was the following month that they were to run away. She would leave Yonville as though going to Rouen to run errands. Rodolphe would have reserved the seats, obtained passports, and even written to Paris so that they might have the whole mail coach to themselves as far as Marseilles, where they would buy a calèche and, from there, continue without stopping along the road to Genoa. She would have taken care to send her luggage to Lheureux’s, from where it would be carried directly to the Hirondelle, so that no one would have any suspicions; and, in all of this, her child was never mentioned. Rodolphe avoided speaking of her; perhaps Emma did not think of her.

He wanted to have another two weeks before him to finish making a few arrangements; then, after a week, he asked for another fifteen days; then he said that he was ill; next he went on a journey; the month of August passed, and, after all these delays, they settled that it would irrevocably be on September 4, a Monday.

At last Saturday, the day before the day before, arrived.

Rodolphe came in the evening, earlier than usual.

“Is everything ready?” she asked him.

“Yes.”

Then they walked around a flower bed and went to sit near the terrace, on the coping of the wall.

“You are sad,” Emma said.

“No, why?”

And yet he was looking at her strangely, tenderly.

“Is it because you are going away?” she resumed. “Because you are leaving those you love, your life? Ah! I understand... But I, I have nothing in the world! You are everything to me. And so I shall be everything to you; I shall be a family to you, a homeland; I shall care for you, I shall love you.”

“How charming you are!” he said, seizing her in his arms.

“Truly?” she said with a voluptuous laugh. “Do you love me? Swear it, then!”

“If I love you! If I love you! Why, I adore you, my love!”

The moon, perfectly round and purple in color, was rising level with the ground at the far end of the meadow. It climbed swiftly among the branches of the poplars, which concealed it here and there like a black curtain pierced with holes. Then it appeared, dazzlingly white, in the empty sky that it illuminated; and then, slowing, it cast a great patch upon the river, making an infinity of stars; and that silvery gleam seemed to writhe there down to the depths, like a headless snake covered in luminous scales. It also resembled some monstrous candelabrum from which drops of molten diamond streamed all along its length. The mild night spread out around them; sheets of shadow filled the foliage. Emma, her eyes half closed, drew in the cool blowing wind with deep sighs. They did not speak to each other, so lost were they in the flood of their reverie. The tenderness of former days returned to their hearts, abundant and silent like the flowing river, with as much softness as the fragrance of the mock orange brought with it, and cast upon their memory shadows more immense and more melancholy than those of the motionless willows stretching over the grass. Often some nocturnal creature, a hedgehog or a weasel, setting out to hunt, disturbed the leaves, or now and then they heard a ripe peach fall by itself from the espalier.

“Ah! What a beautiful night!” Rodolphe said.

“We shall have others!” Emma replied.

And, as though speaking to herself:

“Yes, it will be delightful to travel... Why is my heart sad, though? Is it apprehension of the unknown... the effect of leaving familiar habits behind... or rather...? No, it is an excess of happiness! How weak I am, am I not? Forgive me!”

“There is still time!” he cried. “Think it over; perhaps you will regret it.”

“Never!” she said impetuously.

And, moving closer to him:

“What misfortune, then, can befall me? There is no desert, no precipice, no ocean that I would not cross with you. As we go on living together, it will be like an embrace growing tighter, more complete, with each passing day! There will be nothing to trouble us, no worries, no obstacle! We shall be alone, wholly each other’s, forever... Speak, then, answer me.”

At regular intervals he answered, “Yes... yes!...” She had run her hands through his hair, and she repeated in a childlike voice, despite the large tears flowing down her cheeks:

“Rodolphe! Rodolphe!... Ah! Rodolphe, dear little Rodolphe!”

Midnight struck.

“Midnight!” she said. “Come, it is tomorrow! Only one more day!”

He rose to leave; and, as though the gesture he made had been the signal for their flight, Emma suddenly assumed a cheerful air:

“You have the passports?”

“Yes.”

“You are not forgetting anything?”

“No.”

“Are you sure?”
